reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Characterised by a non-infected fluid collection in the middle ear behind an intact tympanic membrane, without acute signs of infection
A leading cause of acquired conductive hearing loss in children and often presents as inattention, poor school performance or delayed speech
Frequently follows acute otitis media or arises from persistent Eustachian tube dysfunction, often related to adenoid hypertrophy
Otoscopy may reveal a dull, retracted drum, an air-fluid level or bubbles, and reduced mobility
Tympanometry showing a flat (type B) trace and audiometry demonstrating conductive loss support the diagnosis
In adults, unilateral persistent effusion should prompt examination of the postnasal space to exclude a nasopharyngeal tumour
Many cases resolve spontaneously, so an initial period of watchful waiting with reassessment is appropriate
Persistent effusion with significant hearing loss may be managed with ventilation (grommet) tubes, often alongside adenoidectomy
reference.pathophysiology: Otitis media with effusion results from prolonged Eustachian tube dysfunction that impairs middle ear ventilation. Persistent negative pressure encourages transudation of fluid and metaplasia of the middle ear mucosa toward a secretory epithelium, producing a serous or mucoid (glue-like) effusion. The retained fluid dampens ossicular movement and causes a conductive hearing loss. Contributing factors include adenoid hypertrophy, recurrent upper respiratory infections, allergy, cleft palate and, in adults, nasopharyngeal masses obstructing the tube.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital ossicular or cochlear hearing loss
additionalInvestigations: Pneumatic otoscopy to assess drum mobility
Tympanometry to detect middle ear fluid and negative pressure
Pure tone audiometry to quantify conductive hearing loss
Nasopharyngeal examination or endoscopy in persistent unilateral adult effusion
Assessment of adenoids and allergic or sinonasal contributors
redFlags: Unilateral persistent effusion in an adult raising concern for nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Progressive hearing loss affecting speech and language development in a child
Signs of retraction pocket or cholesteatoma developing
Effusion associated with cranial nerve signs or neck mass
reference.prognosis: The majority of childhood cases resolve spontaneously within weeks to months; persistent disease can impair hearing and language development but generally responds well to ventilation tubes and treatment of underlying causes.
pitfalls: Overprescribing antibiotics for a fundamentally non-infective effusion
Failing to examine the nasopharynx in an adult with unilateral effusion
Intervening surgically too early before allowing spontaneous resolution
Missing associated speech, language or educational impact in children
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Initial period of active observation, since most childhood effusions resolve spontaneously within weeks to months
Insertion of ventilation tubes (grommets) for persistent bilateral effusion with hearing loss affecting speech, language or schooling
Adjuvant adenoidectomy where adenoid hypertrophy contributes, particularly in recurrent disease
Hearing aids as an alternative for persistent hearing loss when surgery is declined or unsuitable
Treat contributing factors such as allergy, sinonasal disease and recurrent upper respiratory infection
In adults, examine the postnasal space and image to exclude a nasopharyngeal tumour when the effusion is unilateral and persistent
Monitor hearing and speech-and-language development with audiometry and tympanometry
